one_liner: Small C++11/14 msgpack-rpc client and server with no IDL; its author's 2017 benchmark has small calls 2.5x faster than gRPC 1.1.0.
what_it_does: rpclib exposes ordinary C++ functions and lambdas over the msgpack-rpc protocol. srv.bind("name", f) captures the signature through templates, srv.run() serves on the calling thread and srv.async_run(n) on n worker threads. On the client, c.call("name", args...).as<T>() blocks, async_call returns a std::future and send() posts a notification. User structs need only an MSGPACK_DEFINE line, and any language with a msgpack-rpc implementation can talk to it. It does not replace gRPC: there is no schema or code generation, no HTTP/2, streaming, TLS, deadlines or load balancing.
how_it_is_fast: It does far less per call than gRPC. A call is one msgpack array [type, msgid, method, params] written over a persistent plain TCP connection, with no HTTP/2 framing, HPACK or protobuf message objects. Standalone Asio reads into a streaming msgpack unpacker that reserves a 1 MiB buffer per connection, the server finds the function by name in a std::unordered_map, converts the result to a msgpack object and packs it into one sbuffer written on an Asio strand. Most of the work runs on the client's I/O thread and the server worker, so the calling thread used only 4.7 µs of CPU per get_answer call against 22.1 µs of wall time.
when_to_use: In-house C++ services, simulators or tools (AirSim is the listed user) that need a quick request/response RPC between processes on one host or a trusted LAN, with almost no boilerplate.
Many small, latency-sensitive calls over one persistent connection, where the benchmark measured about 22 µs per round trip vs about 55 µs for gRPC 1.1.0.
Talking to Python, Node, Go or other msgpack-rpc peers without maintaining .proto or .thrift files.
Old toolchains or C++11 codebases that cannot pull in gRPC's dependency tree: Asio, msgpack-c and fmt are vendored, and the build is a single CMake static library.
when_not_to_use: You need a maintained library: the README says 'rpclib is looking for maintainers' and points to packio, and the last commit was 2022-11-22.

Large payloads: in the same suite Thrift was faster at most blob sizes (1 KB: 14,362 ns vs 23,608 ns) and both Thrift and Cap'n Proto were faster from 256 KB to 16 MB. gRPC's blob rows were never run.
Untrusted networks or public endpoints: there is no TLS or authentication, no documented maximum message size, and the 1 MiB per-connection buffer grows by doubling.
Streaming, cancellation, deadlines, schema evolution or polyglot code generation: none of these exist.
Multithreaded servers whose clients may disconnect mid-call: issue #231 (open since 2019) reports async_run servers crashing when they reply to a client that has gone.

integration.form: static lib (CMake project; Asio, msgpack-c and fmt vendored under the clmdep_ namespaces)
integration.dependencies: none external (standalone Asio, msgpack-c and fmt ship in dependencies/); pthreads on POSIX
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (RPCLIB_CXX_STANDARD 11 by default, 14 allowed) and CMake >= 3.5.1. The changelog lowered the minimum g++ to 4.8 in 2.1.0, while the benchmark suite asks for g++ 5.4 or clang 3.8.
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS and Windows (MSVC) via Asio; MinGW support is an open request (issue #206)
integration.thread_safety: With run(), handlers execute on the thread that called run(). With async_run(n), each decoded call is posted to the io_service, so any worker can run it: calls from one connection can execute concurrently and finish out of order, and bound functions must be thread-safe. The client gives each call an atomic id and serializes writes on a strand, and its own I/O thread completes the futures.

gotchas: Harness flaw that matters for the caveats: the Cap'n Proto get_structs row is not like for like. capnp_code::fill_struct_cache calls initSchools(item_count) but never fills the schools (its random_School lambda is unused). rpclib, Thrift and gRPC each send 34 students with 34 schools of 34 37-character e-mail addresses, which we estimate at about 1.5 MB of the payload. Cap'n Proto's 183,415 ns is 21x faster than the in-process direct_bench deep copy of the same data (3,859,058 ns), so 'rpclib is not faster than Cap'n Proto on get_structs' should not be cited.

The measured build is not a release. benchmark.json is dated 2017-02-20, three weeks before the 1.0.0 tag (2017-03-11), whose changelog lists 'A buffer overflow bug was fixed in the server'. The conan package rpclib/1.0.0@sztomi/testing was a pre-release snapshot of unknown commit, run on a 4-CPU machine with frequency scaling on and no CPU model. The win over gRPC is against gRPC 1.1.0 (January 2017) in its synchronous API, and gRPC's blob benchmark was commented out over grpc issue 9510.

No default client timeout (removed in 2.1.0): call() blocks until a reply arrives unless set_timeout() is used. A timed-out call is not cancelled on the server, because msgpack-rpc has no cancellation.

Each rpc::client starts its own I/O thread, and every client and server session reserves a 1 MiB unpacker buffer (DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE = 1024 << 10). Thousands of connections therefore cost gigabytes of reserved buffers, and the CMake option RPCLIB_DEFAULT_BUFFER_SIZE is the only knob.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick rpclib over brpc or SRPC when you want a tiny, dependency-free C++11 library and msgpack-rpc interoperability rather than a production RPC platform, and over rest_rpc (also msgpack-based, benchmarked against brpc) when existing peers already speak standard msgpack-rpc. If you need to stay wire-compatible with gRPC while going faster, grpcxx is the catalogued choice.
verified_claims_summary: The rpclib author's Google Benchmark suite (rpclib/benchmarks, run 2017-02-20, 5 repetitions of at least 3 s each, 4 CPUs at 2.8 GHz, compiler not stated) timed one synchronous localhost TCP round trip per iteration. rpclib 1.0.0 (pre-release) took 22,115 ns for get_answer vs gRPC 1.1.0's 54,841 ns (2.5x), and 8.31 ms vs 17.68 ms for get_structs, a large nested struct (2.1x). Thrift 0.9.3 with TSimpleServer won get_answer at 10,285 ns, and Cap'n Proto's faster get_structs row sent far less data.
status_note: Abandoned in practice: latest release v2.3.0, last commit 2022-11-22, and an open 'looking for maintainers' notice (issue #273) that recommends packio. It is MIT-licensed, has no external dependencies and is small enough to vendor for trusted-network use, but multithreaded-server crash reports (#175, #231) remain open.
